pos: n. (Jan Rokycana, c. 1396–1471, Hussite theologian and archbishop-elect of Prague)
etymology: Czech Jan from Hebrew Yochanan, the LORD is gracious; Rokycana, of Rokycany, a place-name surname.
biblical_def: Jan Rokycana was the leading theologian of the Utraquist party in Bohemia, the Hussite settlement that held the cup for the laity against Rome and was granted it by the Compacts of Basel. He was elected archbishop of Prague and never confirmed by any pope, preaching for decades in the Tyn church without a see. His sermons on the corruption of the priesthood and the shape of the apostolic church were so searching that a group of his hearers, led by his own kinsman Gregory, concluded that the church he described could not be found in the Bohemia he was defending, and went off in 1457 to form the Unity of the Brethren. Rokycana would not go with them and in the end approved their suppression. The dictionary holds him up for that exact hinge. A man may preach the truth faithfully enough to raise up people who act on it more consistently than he will, and then find himself their opponent. Rokycana's pulpit produced the Brethren and his authority persecuted them.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines utraquist as one who communicates in both kinds, and compact as an agreement or contract between parties.
webster_full: UTRAQUIST, n. One of a sect who communicate in both kinds, receiving both the bread and the cup.
COM'PACT, n. An agreement; a contract between parties; a covenant or convention.
ARCHBISH'OP, n. A chief bishop; a church dignitary of the first class.
CUP, n. A small vessel used to drink out of; the sacramental cup.
scriptures: And he took the cup, and gave thanks, and gave it to them, saying, Drink ye all of it;
After the same manner also he took the cup, when he had supped, saying, This cup is the new testament in my blood: this do ye, as oft as ye drink it, in remembrance of me.
And he took the cup, and when he had given thanks, he gave it to them: and they all drank of it.
Act 2:42
And they continued stedfastly in the apostles' doctrine and fellowship, and in breaking of bread, and in prayers.
corruption_summary: His preaching raised up the Brethren and his authority afterward helped suppress them.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the comfortable idea that a reformer's doctrine and his practice will keep step. Rokycana told Bohemia what the apostolic church looked like, and when men believed him enough to leave the national settlement and build it, he treated them as schismatics. The lesson is not that he was a hypocrite but that it is possible to hold a true principle as a debating position and be unwilling to pay for it.

The principle to recover is the one he did hold and fight for: that the cup belongs to the whole congregation, because Christ gave it to them. “And he took the cup, and gave thanks, and gave it to them, saying, Drink ye all of it” (Mat 26:27). Mark records the obedience: “and they all drank of it” (Mar 14:23). And the standing order of the first church was a shared table — “they continued stedfastly in the apostles' doctrine and fellowship, and in breaking of bread, and in prayers” (Act 2:42).

pos: n. (Jan Augusta, 1500–1572, bishop of the Unity of the Brethren, sixteen years a prisoner)
etymology: Czech Jan from Hebrew Yochanan, the LORD is gracious; Latin Augusta, venerable, majestic.
biblical_def: Jan Augusta was a hatter's apprentice who became the chief bishop of the Unity of the Brethren, and he spent sixteen years of his episcopate in a cell at Krivoklat castle. Arrested in 1548 in the repression that followed the Bohemian estates' defeat, he was tortured, pressed to recant, and held until 1564. He had been eager for union with the Lutherans before his arrest and was never fully trusted by his own church afterward; his years in prison produced hymns, and the Brethren hymnbook he had helped shape went on being sung long after the arguments about him had died. The dictionary records the whole of it, including the suspicion. A church that has had a leader broken in prison does not always know what to do with him when he comes out, and the Brethren's treatment of Augusta after his release is not creditable. What is creditable, and what the entry keeps, is sixteen years in which he did not deny the faith, and the hymns he made in the dark.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines recant as to retract a declaration or opinion, and dungeon as a close dark prison.
webster_full: RECANT', v.t. To retract; to recall; to contradict a former declaration; to unsay.
DUN'GEON, n. A close prison, or a deep dark place of confinement.
BISH'OP, n. An overseer; a spiritual superintendent, ruler or director.
HYMN, n. A song or ode in honour of God; a sacred song.

corruption_summary: Sixteen years in Krivoklat castle without recanting, and hymns written in the cell.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is a romantic view of imprisonment that skips the aftermath. Augusta came out of sixteen years in a cell to find his own church uneasy with him, partly over his old eagerness for a Lutheran union and partly because men who have been broken are awkward company. The dictionary names the unkindness rather than tidying it away.

The principle to recover is that bonds do not bind the word and do not silence praise. “I suffer trouble, as an evil doer, even unto bonds; but the word of God is not bound” (2Ti 2:9). The eleventh of Hebrews lists exactly his portion: “yea, moreover of bonds and imprisonment” (Heb 11:36). At Philippi the answer to a prison was a hymn at midnight — “Paul and Silas prayed, and sang praises unto God: and the prisoners heard them” (Act 16:25) — and the promise to the imprisoned church at Smyrna is the promise Augusta had: “be thou faithful unto death, and I will give thee a crown of life” (Rev 2:10).

pos: n. (Matej Cervenka, 1521–1569, bishop of the Unity of the Brethren, hymnwriter and diarist)
etymology: Czech Matej from Hebrew Mattithyah, gift of the LORD; Cervenka, little red one, a Czech surname.
biblical_def: Matej Cervenka was one of the two men who carried the Unity of the Brethren through the years when Augusta was in prison, the other being Jan Blahoslav. He served as a bishop, wrote and edited hymns for the Brethren hymnbooks, kept a diary that is one of the chief sources for the Unity's inner life, and had a hand in presenting the Brethren's confession of faith to the Protestant churches of Germany and Switzerland. That confession work mattered. The Brethren were a small, old and easily misrepresented body — descended from the Hussites, organised before Luther, with a discipline stricter than any Lutheran or Reformed church — and they were repeatedly accused of being Anabaptists or worse. Cervenka's labour was to set down in a form the Wittenbergers and the Swiss could read exactly what the Brethren believed, and so to purchase recognition for a church that had none. The dictionary values a confession written to end a slander.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines confession as a formulary comprising the articles of faith, and diary as an account of daily events.
webster_full: CONFES'SION, n. A formulary in which the articles of faith are comprised; a creed to be assented to or signed.
DI'ARY, n. A register of daily events or transactions; a journal.
SLAN'DER, n. A false tale or report maliciously uttered, tending to injure the reputation of another.
U'NITY, n. The state of being one; concord; conjunction.
scriptures: But sanctify the Lord God in your hearts: and be ready always to give an answer to every man that asketh you a reason of the hope that is in you with meekness and fear:
Having your conversation honest among the Gentiles: that, whereas they speak against you as evildoers, they may by your good works, which they shall behold, glorify God in the day of visitation.
Hold fast the form of sound words, which thou hast heard of me, in faith and love which is in Christ Jesus.
Let us hold fast the profession of our faith without wavering; (for he is faithful that promised;)
corruption_summary: He set the Brethren's faith down in a confession the German and Swiss churches could read, and ended a slander.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the suspicion of confessions as instruments of exclusion, when their first use is almost always the opposite: a small and misreported body writes down what it believes so that it can be judged by what it actually holds instead of by rumour. The Brethren were called Anabaptists, Donatists and Picards by men who had never read a line of theirs.

The principle to recover is that Christians owe a stated answer for their hope and a visible walk to match it: “be ready always to give an answer to every man that asketh you a reason of the hope that is in you with meekness and fear” (1Pe 3:15). The slandered church answers partly by conduct: “that, whereas they speak against you as evildoers, they may by your good works, which they shall behold, glorify God” (1Pe 2:12). And the form of sound words is to be gripped, not improvised — “Hold fast the form of sound words” (2Ti 1:13).

pos: n. (Jiri Strejc, 1536–1599, Brethren minister, Czech psalmist and translator of the Kralice Bible)
etymology: Czech Jiri from Greek Georgios, a husbandman; Strejc, an uncle, a kinsman, a Czech surname.
biblical_def: Jiri Strejc, known in Latin as Georgius Vetter, was a minister of the Unity of the Brethren in Moravia who did two things that outlived him. He was one of the translators of the Kralice Bible, the Brethren's six-volume Czech Scriptures made from Hebrew and Greek with commentary and published between 1579 and 1593 — the Czech Bible, as the Authorized Version is the English one, and for three hundred years the standard of the written language. And in 1587 he put the Genevan Psalter into Czech verse, keeping the French tunes, so that Czech-speaking Protestants sang what Geneva, Hungary and the Netherlands sang. The dictionary pairs him deliberately with Albert Szenci Molnar in Hungary and with the Dutch and French psalters: the same melodies, the same hundred and fifty psalms, carried into four or five languages within a generation by men who never met. That is what a confessional communion actually looks like, and it was built out of a text and a tune rather than out of a council.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines psalmody as the practice of singing psalms, and tune as a series of musical notes in a particular measure.
webster_full: PSAL'MODY, n. The act, practice or art of singing sacred songs.
TUNE, n. A series of musical notes in some particular measure, and consisting of a single series.
VER'SION, n. A translation; that which is rendered from another language.
COM'MENTARY, n. A series of comments or annotations; an exposition of a book.

corruption_summary: He translated for the Kralice Bible and set the Genevan Psalter to Czech verse in 1587.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the assumption that Christian unity has to be organised from a centre. Nobody organised the spread of the Genevan Psalter. Czech, Hungarian, Dutch, German and English congregations ended up singing the same tunes to the same hundred and fifty psalms because each independently judged that the Psalter is the church's songbook and the tunes were serviceable.

The principle to recover is that the Psalms are given for all nations to sing and that singing them is itself a confession of one faith. “O sing unto the LORD a new song: sing unto the LORD, all the earth” (Psa 96:1). The shortest psalm commands it of the heathen: “O praise the LORD, all ye nations: praise him, all ye people” (Psa 117:1). And the end of it is seen in John's vision of “a great multitude, which no man could number, of all nations, and kindreds, and people, and tongues” (Rev 7:9).

pos: n. (Simeon Teofil Turnovsky, 1544–1608, senior of the Brethren in Poland and architect of the Sandomierz Consensus)
etymology: Hebrew Shimon, hearing; Greek Theophilos, lover of God; Turnovsky, of Turnov, a place-name surname.
biblical_def: Simeon Teofil Turnovsky led the Polish branch of the Unity of the Brethren, which had taken root in Great Poland after the Bohemian expulsions, and he gave much of his life to one object: a working agreement between the Reformed, the Lutherans and the Brethren in Poland. The Consensus of Sandomierz of 1570 was largely his achievement, and he spent the following decades defending it against those on all three sides who thought it conceded too much. He also wrote on church order and kept up correspondence across the Protestant world. The dictionary names him for the character of that work. Turnovsky did not pretend the three churches agreed about the Supper; the Consensus sets out each position and then declares that the parties recognise one another as true churches of Christ. That is harder than either fusion or separation, and it is a model the dictionary commends: say plainly what you believe, say plainly where you differ, and then decide on biblical grounds whether the difference unchurches the other man.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines consensus as agreement of minds, and recognition as the acknowledgment of a thing as valid.
webster_full: CONSENT', n. Agreement of minds in opinion; accord; concord.
RECOGNI'TION, n. Acknowledgment; formal avowal; knowledge confessed or avowed.
SEN'IOR, n. One older in office or in age; the chief officer of a body of ministers.
COM'MUNION, n. Fellowship; intercourse between two persons or more; mutual participation.

corruption_summary: The Sandomierz Consensus of 1570 was largely his: three churches naming their differences and recognising each other.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the two easy options. One is fusion, which buys agreement by refusing to state anything; the other is separation, which treats every difference as fatal. Sandomierz did neither: it printed the three positions on the Supper, declined to harmonise them, and then said that these are churches of Christ and will behave toward each other as such.

The principle to recover is that recognition rests on what Christ has received, not on what we find comfortable. “Wherefore receive ye one another, as Christ also received us to the glory of God” (Rom 15:7). Walking together presupposes real agreement about real things — “Can two walk together, except they be agreed?” (Amo 3:3) — and where the attainment is partial, Paul's rule is to hold the ground gained: “let us walk by the same rule, let us mind the same thing” (Phi 3:16).

pos: n. (Jan Turnowski, 1567–1629, senior of the Brethren in Poland and co-reviser of the Gdansk Bible)
etymology: Czech and Polish Jan from Hebrew Yochanan, the LORD is gracious; Turnowski, of Turnov, a place-name surname.
biblical_def: Jan Turnowski succeeded to the leadership of the Brethren's Polish congregations and worked with the Reformed minister Daniel Mikolajewski on the revision of the Polish Scriptures printed at Gdansk in 1632, which became the Polish Protestant Bible for three centuries. He was a preacher and a hymn editor as well, and he held the Brethren's Polish churches together in the decades when the Counter-Reformation was recovering the Commonwealth parish by parish. The dictionary pairs his entry with Mikolajewski's on purpose. Two men of two different churches, which had agreed at Sandomierz to recognise one another without pretending to agree about the Supper, sat down together over the Hebrew and the Greek and produced one Bible for both their peoples. The fruit of a limited and honest union was a text that outlasted both communions in Poland. The dictionary knows no better argument for doing unity that way.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines revision as the act of reviewing and correcting, and collaborate as to labour jointly with others.
webster_full: REVI'SION, n. The act of reviewing; review; re-examination for correction.
COLLAB'ORATOR, n. An associate in labour, especially in literary or scientific pursuits.
SEN'IOR, n. The chief officer of a body of ministers; one older in office.
ED'ITION, n. The publication of a book; one impression or printing of a work.

corruption_summary: A Brother and a Reformed minister revised the Polish Bible together and printed it at Gdansk in 1632.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the assumption that co-operation between churches requires one of them to stop being what it is. Turnowski remained a Brother and Mikolajewski remained Reformed, and the Bible they made together was used by both and by the Polish Lutherans as well.

The principle to recover is that God appoints shared labour and gives it a reward neither man could earn alone. “Two are better than one; because they have a good reward for their labour” (Ecc 4:9). Strength is in the joining: “and a threefold cord is not quickly broken” (Ecc 4:12). The end of such labour is one voice in worship — “That ye may with one mind and one mouth glorify God” (Rom 15:6) — and what it produced outlasted both churches in that land: “but the word of our God shall stand for ever” (Isa 40:8).

pos: n. (Vaclav Budovec z Budova, 1551–1621, Brethren nobleman, author of the Antialkoran, executed at Prague)
etymology: Czech Vaclav, more glory; Budovec z Budova, of Budov, a Bohemian noble house.
biblical_def: Vaclav Budovec z Budova was a Bohemian nobleman of the Unity of the Brethren who spent years at the imperial embassy in Constantinople, learned what he could of the Turkish religion at first hand, and wrote the Antialkoran, a Czech examination of the Koran's claims measured against the Scriptures. He was one of the chief authors of the Letter of Majesty of 1609, by which the Emperor Rudolf granted the Bohemian Protestants legal liberty of worship, and a leader of the estates in the rising that followed its violation. After the Battle of the White Mountain he was arrested at the age of seventy, and on the twenty-first of June 1621 he was beheaded with twenty-six others in the Old Town Square of Prague. The dictionary keeps him at full length. He had argued against Islam from Scripture, won his nation a charter of religious liberty on paper, watched the charter torn up, and died for the church that charter had protected — an old man in a public square, which is where most charters end.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines charter as a written instrument granting rights or privileges, and apostasy from the faith as a forsaking of what was professed.
webster_full: CHAR'TER, n. A written instrument, executed with usual forms, given as evidence of a grant or privileges.
MAJ'ESTY, n. Greatness of appearance; dignity; title of emperors, kings and queens.
SCAF'FOLD, n. A temporary gallery or stage raised for the execution of a criminal.
AL'CORAN, n. The Mohammedan bible or book, containing the religion of Mohammed.

corruption_summary: He wrote against the Koran, won the Letter of Majesty in 1609, and was beheaded at Prague in 1621.
corruption_paragraphs: The error Budovec set himself against is the claim of the Koran to supersede the gospel, and the dictionary states the issue as he did: a later book which denies that God has a Son and that the Son died and rose cannot be a further revelation from the God of the Scriptures, because it contradicts the only revelation He has given. The modern instinct is to compare the two religions as parallel traditions. Budovec, who had lived in Constantinople, compared them as competing claims about one Jesus of Nazareth, and judged accordingly.

The standard is the exclusiveness of Christ, which the New Testament states without a hedge. “I am the way, the truth, and the life: no man cometh unto the Father, but by me” (Joh 14:6). “Neither is there salvation in any other: for there is none other name under heaven given among men, whereby we must be saved” (Act 4:12). And against any later gospel, from any source, Paul fixes the rule: “though we, or an angel from heaven, preach any other gospel unto you than that which we have preached unto you, let him be accursed” (Gal 1:8). Budovec held it to the scaffold — “be thou faithful unto death, and I will give thee a crown of life” (Rev 2:10).

pos: n. (Karel the Elder of Zerotin, 1564–1636, Moravian Brethren nobleman and protector of the Unity)
etymology: Czech Karel from Germanic Karl, a free man; Zerotin, of Zerotin, a Moravian noble house.
biblical_def: Karel the Elder of Zerotin was the greatest Moravian nobleman of his generation, a member of the Unity of the Brethren, educated at Strasbourg and Basel, and for a time governor of Moravia. He judged the Bohemian rising of 1618 to be rash and would not join it, and when it ended at the White Mountain he was one of very few Protestant magnates left with any standing. He used it. He sheltered Brethren ministers on his estates, including the young Jan Amos Comenius, for as long as the law allowed, and when the expulsions came he went into exile himself at Wroclaw rather than conform. The dictionary records his judgment and his cost together. Zerotin declined to put the church into a war he thought unwinnable, was proved right, and was ruined anyway. Prudence is a Christian virtue and it is not a shelter; a man may read the times correctly and still lose his country.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines prudence as wisdom applied to practice, and protector as one who defends or shields from injury.
webster_full: PRU'DENCE, n. Wisdom applied to practice; that discretion which enables a man to judge what is best to be done.
PROTECT'OR, n. One who defends or shields from injury, oppression or danger.
GOV'ERNOR, n. One who governs; one invested with supreme authority in a state or province.
SEQUES'TRATE, v.t. To seize and detain the property of another; to confiscate.

(Of whom the world was not worthy:) they wandered in deserts, and in mountains, and in dens and caves of the earth.
corruption_summary: He refused the rising of 1618, was proved right, sheltered Brethren ministers, and was ruined and exiled anyway.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the belief that discernment protects a man — that reading the situation correctly is a kind of insurance. Zerotin read 1618 exactly right, said so, kept out of it, and lost his estates and his country when the reckoning came anyway, because the victors did not sort Protestants by whether they had been prudent.

The principle to recover is that prudence is commanded and is not a promise of safety. “A prudent man foreseeth the evil, and hideth himself: but the simple pass on, and are punished” (Pro 22:3). The simple believe every word; the prudent man looks well to his going (Pro 14:15). And the prudent may still finish among those of whom the world was not worthy, who “wandered in deserts, and in mountains, and in dens and caves of the earth” (Heb 11:38). Meanwhile the duty is plain for a man with any standing left: “Open thy mouth for the dumb in the cause of all such as are appointed to destruction” (Pro 31:8).

pos: n. (Jan Cyrill Trebicsky, c. 1560–1632, senior of the Unity of the Brethren who crowned Frederick V at Prague)
etymology: Czech Jan from Hebrew Yochanan, the LORD is gracious; Greek Kurillos, lordly.
biblical_def: Jan Cyrill Trebicsky was a senior of the Unity of the Brethren and the administrator of the Utraquist consistory in the brief Protestant ascendancy in Bohemia, and in November 1619 he placed the crown on Frederick of the Palatinate in St Vitus' cathedral. Thirteen months later Frederick had lost the battle and the kingdom, and Cyrill, by then an old man, went into exile with the rest of the Brethren's ministry; his daughter had married Jan Amos Comenius. The dictionary records the coronation without celebrating it. The Bohemian estates had elected a Protestant king in the hope of securing the church by securing the throne, and within a year the throne was gone, the church was proscribed, and the kingdom entered thirty years of war. A minister who crowns a king has staked the gospel's standing in his country on a political outcome, and this is the clearest instance in Reformation history of how that wager settles.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines coronation as the act of crowning a sovereign, and consistory as an assembly of ecclesiastical persons.
webster_full: CORONA'TION, n. The act or solemnity of crowning a king or queen; the pomp or assembly at a coronation.
CONSIS'TORY, n. A place of justice in the spiritual court; an assembly of ecclesiastical persons.
SEN'IOR, n. The chief officer of a body of ministers; one older in office.
PROSCRI'BE, v.t. To put out of the protection of law; to outlaw; to condemn as dangerous.

Some trust in chariots, and some in horses: but we will remember the name of the LORD our God.

Thus saith the LORD; Cursed be the man that trusteth in man, and maketh flesh his arm, and whose heart departeth from the LORD.

And he changeth the times and the seasons: he removeth kings, and setteth up kings: he giveth wisdom unto the wise, and knowledge to them that know understanding:
corruption_summary: He crowned Frederick V in 1619 and was in exile within two years, the church proscribed with the king.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is a perennial one and not peculiar to Bohemia: the church putting her security into the hands of a candidate and calling the arrangement providence. The estates chose Frederick because he was Reformed; the Brethren's senior crowned him; and the whole Protestant establishment of Bohemia was swept away with him in a single season because it had been tied to him.

The principle to recover is that God alone sets up and removes kings, and that trust placed in any of them is misplaced. “Put not your trust in princes, nor in the son of man, in whom there is no help” (Psa 146:3). “Some trust in chariots, and some in horses: but we will remember the name of the LORD our God” (Psa 20:7). The curse is explicit: “Cursed be the man that trusteth in man, and maketh flesh his arm” (Jer 17:5). And the authority is His — “he removeth kings, and setteth up kings” (Dan 2:21).

pos: n. (Matous Konecny, 1569–1622, bishop of the Unity of the Brethren at Mlada Boleslav)
etymology: Czech Matous from Hebrew Mattithyah, gift of the LORD; Konecny, final, last, a Czech surname.
biblical_def: Matous Konecny was a bishop of the Unity of the Brethren at Mlada Boleslav and the author of practical Czech divinity for ordinary households, including a long work on the duties of the Christian estates — magistrates, ministers, parents, children, masters, servants. He died in 1622, in the first wave of the Bohemian proscription, and before the end he had his library and papers walled up in the Brethren house at Mlada Boleslav. They were found in 2006, four centuries later: hundreds of books and letters bricked into a cavity by men who expected to come back. The dictionary ends this batch there deliberately. A church being destroyed hid its books in a wall, and the men who laid the bricks were wrong about returning and right about the books. Konecny's own subject was the ordinary Christian calling — how a father, a servant or a magistrate serves God in the place he is set — and that is what survived the wall.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines calling as one's usual occupation or employment, and immure as to shut up within walls.
webster_full: CALL'ING, n. A proper or usual occupation or employment; the divine summons to a station in life.
IMMU'RE, v.t. To wall in; to enclose within walls; to shut up; to confine.
ES'TATE, n. Condition or circumstances of any person or thing; a rank or order in a commonwealth.
LI'BRARY, n. A collection of books belonging to a private person or to a public institution.
scriptures: Brethren, let every man, wherein he is called, therein abide with God.
Eph 6:5
Servants, be obedient to them that are your masters according to the flesh, with fear and trembling, in singleness of your heart, as unto Christ;
Col 3:23
And whatsoever ye do, do it heartily, as to the Lord, and not unto men;

Thus saith the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel; Take these evidences, this evidence of the purchase, both which is sealed, and this evidence which is open; and put them in an earthen vessel, that they may continue many days.
corruption_summary: He wrote on the ordinary Christian callings, and had the Brethren library bricked into a wall in 1622.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the modern separation of the spiritual life from the ordinary calling, so that a servant, a father or a town councillor looks for his religion in what he does after work. Konecny wrote a whole volume on the opposite: the duties of each estate, performed as service to Christ, are the Christian life for most Christians most of the time.

The principle to recover is that God assigns a station and is served in it. “Brethren, let every man, wherein he is called, therein abide with God” (1Co 7:24). Even bondservice is turned into worship: “And whatsoever ye do, do it heartily, as to the Lord, and not unto men” (Col 3:23). And the hiding of the books has a biblical shape, for Jeremiah too was told to seal the deeds of a doomed country and store them against a future he would not see: “and put them in an earthen vessel, that they may continue many days” (Jer 32:14).
